accepted_phrases: The three frozen bar pages establish seller fields rather than independent taste results. Valrhona SKU B09LMGQFTL is 7.89 dollars, rated 100 percent over two reviews, and marketed in its title as a 70-gram 65-percent single-origin Madagascar bar with tangy and fruity notes, while the same page also lists Manjari as 64 percent; that internal inconsistency remains unresolved. Quma SKU B09PMD2B73 is 9.99 dollars with no reviews shown and is marketed as 70-percent dark chocolate with puffed quinoa, made in Peru, minimally processed, and retaining fruity Criollo aromas; no exact bar mass is established by the page. Pump Street SKU B00VAR0GHY is 12.99 dollars, rated 100 percent over one review, and described as a 70-gram Ecuador dark-milk 60-percent bar with balanced cacao and creamy milk notes. These titles, aggregates and descriptions do not independently establish exact composition, origin traceability, genotype, sensory intensity, recipient preference, ingredients, allergens, freshness, or current delivered cost.

The two frozen box pages establish seller assertions, not recipient fit. Lindt SKU B08H2TSBPX is 19.99 dollars with no reviews shown and describes a 15.2-ounce gift box of approximately 36 individually wrapped milk, dark, white, 60-percent extra-dark, fudge-swirl and sea-salt truffles. Cravings by Zoe SKU B09LM3H2F5 is 24.95 dollars, rated 92 percent over 12 reviews, and describes a 7.5-ounce box of 16 milk-, dark- and white-chocolate shells with assorted fillings including Amaretto, Caramel, Champagne, Coffee, Hazelnut, Irish Cream, Raspberry, Sea Salt Caramel and Tiramisu. Neither page gives a verified dark-piece allocation, cacao percentage for every shell, complete per-piece ingredient and allergen mapping, recipient preference result, current delivered total, or controlled comparison with the three bars.

The dark-chocolate page says cacao percentage is the combined share of chocolate liquor and cocoa butter, with nearly all the rest usually sugar, while the liquor-to-butter split is not disclosed by the percentage. It says identical percentages can therefore have very different compositions and characteristics and that bean-quality variation can make a lower-percentage chocolate more desirable than a higher-percentage one. Percentage is meaningful composition metadata but not a direct quality or preference rank. A 60-percent dark-milk bar, 64-versus-65-percent seller conflict, 70-percent quinoa bar, mixed truffle assortment, and the recipient's usual 85-percent plain bar are not interchangeable formats and must be compared with recipe and product type preserved.

The evidence supports real possible flavor variation without making an origin label deterministic. Dark chocolate can show several flavors, with variation especially noticeable among single-origin products. Flavor cocoa may come from a region, crop or variety or use specific fermentation and harvesting techniques; its assessments include genetics, acidity, fermentation, drying, disease, mold and flavor and combine objective and subjective judgments. Single-origin can cover anything from a country to a plantation and does not necessarily mean one bean type. Fermentation develops flavor precursors later expressed during roasting and reduces bitterness. Traditional Forastero, Criollo and Trinitario categories remain common in marketing but are no longer treated as having a botanical basis. Origin, percentage, genotype, growing conditions, fermentation, drying, roasting, recipe and processing can matter, but no label alone predicts this recipient's flavor ranking.

A traditional chocolate truffle has a ganache center and a coating, and named styles can use cream, butter, dark or milk chocolate, condensed milk, liqueur, buttercream, nut paste, milk powder or other fats. Therefore a truffle-box piece is not equivalent to an unfilled dark bar segment, and total box mass or piece count does not reveal its share of recipient-acceptable dark chocolate. For both exact boxes, verify piece allocation, shell type and percentage, filling, ingredient, allergen, alcohol, freshness and storage information before comparing them with plain bars for a recipient who normally keeps 85-percent bars.

The Jersey City thread asks for handmade chocolates shipped as a birthday gift and contains one commenter saying boxes of a business's truffles went over pretty well. The Pennsylvania thread remembers a large variety of interesting flavors selected into a clear box but never resolves the company identity. The LifeProTips thread proposes chocolate chips as a lower price-per-ounce candy substitute, while comments say all chocolate prices rose, one person prefers semisweet because milk is too sweet and dark too sharp, and another disputes mass-market quality. These author-, business-, time-, product- and preference-scoped statements identify gifting, assortment, price, sweetness and format variables; they are not controlled tests, market rates, exact-offer histories, recipient verdicts, or evidence that a bigger box is more generous in useful servings.

For every current exact offer, record seller and SKU, product form, total mass and count, price and shipping, rating and review count only as seller fields, literal origin and percentage labels including conflicts, plain-bar versus dark-milk versus filled-truffle recipe, dark-piece allocation, ingredients, allergens, alcohol and fillings, stock, arrival date, heat protection, storage and return or replacement terms. Compute cost per recipient-acceptable dark serving after unwanted assortment and waste. When feasible, buy only a reversible small quantity and compare equal coded portions of the bar candidates against the recipient's known 85-percent reference in randomized or blinded order under the same temperature and serving conditions with predeclared aroma, bitterness, acidity, fruit, texture and overall-preference thresholds. A short trial informs this recipient under tested conditions and does not prove a universal origin, percentage, brand or future-lot winner.

The packet supports neither an automatic single-origin winner nor a larger-box winner. Treat origin and cacao percentage as meaningful but incomplete metadata, preserve the unresolved Valrhona 64-versus-65-percent conflict, keep traditional variety terms at marketing scope, and reject ratings, awards, premium wording, piece count, package size and community anecdotes as recipient-fit proof. Verify exact recipes, dark share, ingredients, allergens, alcohol, delivered cost and arrival protections, calculate cost per acceptable dark serving, and use a small matched tasting against the recipient's known 85-percent reference. Choose only the cheapest exact gift path clearing every budget, recipient darkness, format, ingredient, allergen, delivery and taste gate; otherwise buy a small known 85-percent reference for calibration or defer. Do not name a universal origin, percentage, bar, truffle box or brand winner.

Treat origin and cacao percentage as meaningful but incomplete metadata, preserve product-form and seller-label conflicts, and choose only the cheapest exact gift path that passes budget, recipient darkness, format, ingredient, allergen, delivery and matched-taste gates; otherwise use a small known 85-percent reference or defer.

Reject ratings, awards, larger-box presentation, origin and percentage labels as automatic recipient-fit proof; select the least costly exact gift only after every predeclared gate passes, and otherwise buy a known 85-percent calibration reference or defer without a universal winner.

The packet contains five frozen seller snapshots, general percentage, origin, fermentation, variety and truffle context, and three scoped community discussions, but lacks current delivered totals and arrival verification, complete dark-piece, ingredient, allergen and alcohol fields for every offer, and a matched recipient tasting.

Seller titles, SKUs, prices, ratings, review counts, masses, counts, origin, percentage, flavor and gift descriptions remain frozen assertions rather than independent composition, traceability, taste or recipient-fit proof.
The Valrhona page's 65-percent title and quick-look wording conflict with its 64-percent Manjari option, so the exact percentage must remain unresolved until independently verified.

Cacao percentage combines chocolate liquor and cocoa butter without disclosing their split, and identical percentages can have different compositions, so percentage cannot directly rank flavor or recipient fit.

Origin can scope real variation while genetics, growing conditions, fermentation, drying, roasting, recipe and processing also affect possible flavor, and no single label predicts the recipient's ranking.
Traditional Criollo, Forastero and Trinitario terms remain marketing language rather than current botanical proof of an exact product's genotype or quality.

A filled and coated truffle is not equivalent to a plain dark-bar portion, so box mass and piece count do not establish recipient-acceptable dark servings without shell, filling, percentage, ingredient, allergen and alcohol details.

Gift success, flavor-variety, price-per-ounce and sweetness comments remain author-, business-, product-, time- and preference-scoped rather than controlled tests, current rates or exact-offer verdicts.
Current delivered cost, stock, arrival, heat protection, storage, remedy terms, full ingredients, allergens and alcohol must be verified before purchase.
Compare cost per recipient-acceptable dark serving after shipping, unwanted assortment and waste rather than sticker price, total mass or box count alone.

A higher cacao percentage always means higher chocolate quality and better flavor.
The 70-percent bar automatically wins because its number is closest among the candidates to the recipient's usual 85-percent bar.

One Jersey City comment that truffle gifts went over well is a controlled test of the two exact captured boxes for this sister.

The frozen product pages prove current stock, delivered total, birthday arrival, heat protection and replacement terms.
The buyer should purchase the biggest box even if ingredient, allergen, alcohol and dark-share fields remain unresolved.
Single-origin bars always beat assorted truffle boxes, or assorted truffle boxes always beat single-origin bars, for every dark-chocolate lover.

research_subgoals.description: Audit the three exact bar snapshots, retain the Manjari 64-versus-65-percent conflict, distinguish plain dark, dark-milk and added-ingredient forms, and explain why percentage and seller ratings do not directly rank quality or recipient fit.

Audit the two exact assorted-truffle boxes and truffle structure, then identify the dark-share, shell, filling, ingredient, allergen and alcohol fields required before box size or count can represent recipient-useful generosity.

Explain how origin, genetics, growing conditions, fermentation, drying, roasting, recipe and processing can produce real flavor variation while refusing deterministic origin, percentage or traditional-variety label claims.
Keep the three community discussions at their author, business, product, time, price and preference scopes while extracting only gift, assortment, cost, sweetness and format variables to verify.

Combine every evidence branch into an exact-offer matrix, current delivery and safety audit, cost-per-acceptable-dark-serving calculation, and small matched tasting against the recipient's known 85-percent reference.

Choose only the cheapest exact gift path passing all budget, recipient darkness, format, ingredient, allergen, delivery and taste gates, or use a small known 85-percent reference or defer without a universal bar, box, origin or percentage winner.
